questions.question: What is the core idea of a Vision Transformer?
options: Apply convolutions with very large kernels
Split the image into patches and treat each patch as a token in a Transformer, like words in a sentence
Process the image one pixel at a time with a recurrent network
Convert the image to text with OCR first
questions.explanation: ViT cuts the image into fixed-size patches (e.g. 16x16) and treats each as a 'visual word' token, then feeds the sequence to a standard Transformer. Hence the paper title 'An Image is Worth 16x16 Words'.

questions.question: For a 224x224 image with patch size 16, how many patch tokens are there, and how many total tokens does ViT-B/16 use?
options: 256 patches, 257 total
196 patches, 197 total (with the CLS token)
14 patches, 15 total
49 patches, 50 total
questions.explanation: N = (224 x 224) / (16 x 16) = 50176 / 256 = 196 patches (a 14x14 grid). Adding the prepended [CLS] token gives 197 total tokens.

questions.question: Why does a ViT need positional embeddings?
options: To normalize the pixel values
Self-attention is order-blind (permutation-invariant), so without them the model can't tell where each patch came from
To reduce the number of parameters
To convert patches to grayscale
questions.explanation: Attention treats tokens as an unordered set. Positional embeddings are added to each token so the model knows each patch's location in the image, preserving spatial structure.

questions.question: Self-attention over N tokens has what computational complexity, and why does this matter for ViT?
options: O(N), so resolution is free
O(N^2 D) — every pair of tokens is compared, which is why patches (196) are used instead of pixels (50176)
O(log N), negligible
O(D) only, independent of N
questions.explanation: Attention compares every pair of tokens: O(N^2 D). With pixels as tokens N=50176 and N^2 is ~2.5 billion — impossible. Using 16x16 patches gives N=196, making it cheap. Doubling patches quadruples the cost.

questions.question: Compared to a CNN, when do Vision Transformers tend to win?
options: On tiny datasets trained from scratch
When trained/pretrained on very large datasets — ViTs have weaker inductive bias so they're data-hungry but have a higher ceiling
They always win regardless of data
Only on grayscale images
questions.explanation: CNNs have built-in inductive biases (locality, translation-equivariance) making them data-efficient and better on small data. ViTs lack these priors so they need lots of data, but with large-scale pretraining they surpass CNNs. That's why you use pretrained ViTs.
